claims.text: Adding a small concentration of yttrium to a high-entropy-alloy bond coat will improve coating durability and reliability under high-temperature cyclic conditions.
The durability improvement from yttrium addition will result from stronger oxide-scale adhesion.
Undoped high-entropy-alloy bond coats typically form relatively porous or weakly adherent oxide scales during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 0.5–1 at.% yttrium during alloy synthesis.
The synthesis process will distribute the yttrium uniformly throughout the bond coat.
During high-temperature exposure, yttrium will segregate to oxide grain boundaries.
Yttrium segregation will refine the oxide-scale microstructure.
Yttrium will promote a more adherent, continuous, and stable oxide layer.
Yttrium reduces void formation in the growing oxide scale.
Reduced grain-boundary mobility and void formation enhance adhesion between the oxide scale and the bond coat.
Improved oxide/bond-coat interfacial integrity minimizes spallation during thermal cycling.
Yttrium-doped bond coats will exhibit a lower oxide-scale spallation rate than undoped bond coats.
Yttrium-doped bond coats will endure approximately 20–30% more thermal cycles before failure than undoped controls.
The resulting reduction in spallation and increase in cycle life will make TBC performance more reliable.
The beneficial effect should persist under operational temperatures and cyclic stresses typical of turbine applications.
Extreme thermal loads or chemically aggressive environments may diminish the beneficial effect of yttrium or require further optimization.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule is logically ambiguous because it states that either less than a 20% cycle-life increase or improved oxide adhesion would falsify the hypothesis. Improved adhesion is itself a predicted benefit and therefore should support, rather than falsify, at least part of the hypothesis.
